Up to $150 MILLION a year at risk—and an internal government memo basically admits they can’t stop it. 🚨💰

A bombshell ProPublica investigation just uncovered a 25-page internal Labor Department memo detailing the agency’s inability to police fraud in the federal program meant to care for civilian contractors wounded in war zones.

Under the system, private insurers pay out war-hazard injury claims and then bill the U.S. government for reimbursement. Between 2018 and 2024, insurer reimbursement applications jumped eightfold—from around 1,000 to more than 8,000—with billions flowing to major carriers since 2014.

Meanwhile, the memo warns that questionable medical evidence is often overlooked, insurers sometimes settle dubious claims fast knowing taxpayers will reimburse them, and one former top official estimates up to $150 million every year is at risk.

The Labor Department says its hands are tied by decades-old laws and that real reform requires Congress to act.

Why do government reimbursement programs keep getting left wide open to abuse before anyone fixes the rules? Drop your take below. 👇

KHILLIGAY, Afghanistan – U.S. Army Sgt. Joshua R. Labbe of the 10th Mountain Division's 1st Brigade Combat Team received the Silver Star medal, the nation's third highest award for valor in combat, on Feb. 16, during a ceremony at Forward Operating Base Khilligay in northern Afghanistan.

Labbe, from Stonington, Conn., an infantry squad leader with 1st Battalion, 87th Infantry Regiment, is credited with saving the life of one soldier and protecting numerous soldiers during a complex attack that lasted more than six hours.

“We are here to recognize the sacrifice and courage of the soldiers and leaders in Shafi Khel on Oct. 6,” said Lt. Col. Russell Lewis, 1-87 commander, said during the ceremony. “Sgt. Labbe is a hero. He didn't go out on Oct. 6 to earn an award — he just did his job. Except his job that day called for extraordinary actions and he stepped up and helped his comrades.”

On Oct. 6, 2010, Labbe's platoon was conducting a joint combat patrol in the village of Shafi Khel, Baghlan province, Afghanistan, with their Afghan national security force partners.

While establishing an observation post on a hilltop, Labbe and soldiers from 1st Squad as well as the mortar team, came under enemy fire. Initially, the enemy attacked the soldiers of 3rd Platoon with rocket-propelled grenades.
“One truck of ours was hit by an RPG,” Labbe said. “When I saw that truck get hit, I immediate started suppressing with the mortar system.”

Over the next four hours, the platoon came under RPG and small arms fire. Labbe directed the soldiers on the hill to return fire with multiple weapons systems. The hilltop then came under sniper fire, forcing Labbe and the other soldiers to take cover in holes they had dug.

Later, Labbe was told to collapse their position on the hilltop and return to the base of the hill where the remainder of his platoon was located.

“I had to get out of my hole and run to the other hole where the mortar system was,” he said. “When I got to the hole, I got everyone one up, got them online, and got everybody ready. As soon as we got out of the hole, we got sniper fire again.”

With three of the five soldiers making it across the hill to the other hole safely, Labbe and Pfc. Parker Radatz had returned to the mortar hole due to the accuracy of the sniper fire. Labbe and Radatz gathered themselves and attempted to get across the hill again.

“I ran to my hole thinking he was right beside me; little did I know he had actually tripped and fell,” Labbe said. “I turned around, and I saw him trying to get his composure to get back up, but he couldn't because there were multiple rounds impacting all around him.”

With complete disregard for his own safety, Labbe ran across the exposed hilltop to the fallen soldier through enemy fire, picked him up, and brought him to safety.

“I just did what I had to in that situation,” Labbe said. “He has people that care for him and love him, I knew I had to go pick him up and get him to safety. It's my job to take care of my men.”

Later, as the platoon moved down the road, the tow bar pulling the battle-damaged vehicle snapped. While Labbe and three soldiers began repairing the tow bar, once again, the platoon came under small arms fire from nearby rooftops and walls. Labbe immediately returned fire with his M4 rifle.

The small arms fire discontinued for a moment, allowing Labbe to run back to his vehicle to retrieve an M249 machine gun. He moved to a position allowing him to pull security down the alleyway and the walls where they had received fire. At this point, the enemy hopped over the walls and began engaging the platoon again.

With the enemy less than 20 meters away, Labbe stood completely exposed on the road and continued to shield the recovery crew as he fired the machine gun from his shoulder. After expending the 200-round ammunition pouch, he fired the weapon using his 30-round M4 rifle magazines.

“I engaged them for roughly two minutes and continued to pull security until the tow bar was fixed,” he said.

Once the vehicle was recovered, 3rd Platoon continued down the road, where they were ambushed. While still in close contact with the enemy, another vehicle suddenly plunged into an irrigation ditch. Labbe immediately dismounted and moved under fire to the stuck vehicle.

He coordinated the evacuation and recovery of the vehicle while still being engaged with RPG and machinegun fire from compounds and tree lines from less than 100 meters away. Labbe remained exposed to the enemy until the rest of the platoon recovered the vehicle and mounted back in their trucks.

“I feel honored to receive the Silver Star,” he said. “However, I don't think just my actions alone allowed us to be victorious that day. It was the whole platoon. Everyone who was out there that day played an important role in getting everyone back here alive. I couldn't have done what I did that day without my brothers in 3rd Platoon.”

Over the course of more than six hours of close combat, Labbe went above and beyond the call of duty as a squad leader.

“Today, we recognize his actions because they are not common,” said Lewis. “His actions that day distinguished him from others and truly impacted the outcome of the fight in Shafi Khel.”

Article and photo by Army Sgt. Blair Neelands
1st Brigade Combat Team, 10th Mountain Division Public Affairs
Copyright 2011

The President of the United States of America, authorized by Title 10, Section 8742, U.S.C., awards the Air Force Cross to Senior Airman Jason D. Cunningham for extraordinary heroism in military operations against an opposing armed force while serving as a pararescueman near the village of Marzak in the Paktia Province of Afghanistan on 4 March 2002.

On that proud day, Airman Cunningham was the primary Air Force Combat Search and Rescue medic assigned to a Quick Reaction Force tasked to recover two American servicemen evading capture in austere terrain occupied by massed Al Qaida and Taliban forces.

Shortly before landing, his MH-47E helicopter received accurate rocket-propelled grenade and small arms fire, severely disabling the aircraft and causing it to crash land. The assault force formed a hasty defense and immediately suffered three fatalities and five critical casualties.

Despite effective enemy fire, and at great risk to his own life, Airman Cunningham remained in the burning fuselage of the aircraft in order to treat the wounded. As he moved his patients to a more secure location, mortar rounds began to impact within fifty feet of his position. Disregarding this extreme danger, he continued the movement and exposed himself to enemy fire on seven separate occasions.

When the second casualty collection point was also compromised, in a display of uncommon valor and gallantry, Airman Cunningham braved an intense small arms and rocket-propelled grenade attack while repositioning the critically wounded to a third collection point. Even after he was mortally wounded and quickly deteriorating, he continued to direct patient movement and transferred care to another medic.

In the end, his distinct efforts led to the successful delivery of ten gravely wounded Americans to life-saving medical treatment. Through his extraordinary heroism, superb airmanship, aggressiveness in the face of the enemy, and in the dedication of his service to his country, Senior Airman Cunningham reflected the highest credit upon himself and the United States #AirForce.

The Army just made .50-caliber ammo fly less than half as far — and gunners are calling it a huge win for training.

Standard .50-caliber rounds can travel up to 7,400 meters (about 4.6 miles), which means units often struggle to find firing ranges with enough safety space for live-fire drills. Now, DEVCOM has rolled out new M1181 ball and M1199 tracer reduced-range ammunition designed to destabilize right around Mach 1, shed energy fast, and drop much sooner.

That means M2 crews can now run realistic .50-caliber live-fire and convoy exercises on standard 7.62mm ranges that were previously off-limits — giving soldiers more trigger time without sacrificing safety.

Any former or active-duty M2 gunners here? Would this have meant way more range days for your unit? Sound off below.

#USArmy #Military #50Cal

Just days after U.S. strikes in the Strait of Hormuz, sources say Washington and Jerusalem are weighing an even bigger move against Iran. 🚨🌍

According to CBS News, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is pushing for a new joint military operation against Tehran—while it remains unclear how far President Donald Trump is willing to go.

Tensions surged again this week after the U.S. struck Iran’s strategic Qeshm Island in response to Iranian attacks targeting U.S. assets in Bahrain and Kuwait. Iranian leaders have publicly warned that any renewed assault would trigger retaliation far beyond the Gulf, including U.S. bases in Europe, energy infrastructure, and undersea cables.

Meanwhile, the Senate just voted down a war powers resolution to limit Trump’s strike authority—setting up a major clash when the new Congress takes over in January.

Should the U.S. join Israel in a new operation, or focus on de-escalating and reopening the Strait of Hormuz? Drop your take below. 👇

Rifles, tactical gear, and a $13.5 million down payment—Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth just touched down in Honduras with a clear message for cartels. 🇺🇸🇭🇳

Meeting with Honduran President Nasry Asfura on November 19, 2026, Hegseth delivered $13.5 million in military equipment and signed new cyber-defense agreements as part of his Latin America security tour.

"Together, we will stand and defend our hemisphere from narco-terrorists," the Pentagon announcement declared, as Washington expands joint counter-cartel partnerships across the region.

Supporters say arming regional allies is the smartest way to fight cartels before drugs and violence reach the U.S. border—while critics and human rights watchdogs question the legality and long-term impact of U.S. military anti-cartel operations.

Should the U.S. keep sending military gear and funding to Latin American partners to fight cartels? Drop your take below. 👇

#PeteHegseth #Honduras #USMilitary

The Pentagon raised the bar to a single sex-neutral combat standard—and the first numbers from the Marine Corps are turning heads. 🇺🇸💪

Starting in January 2026 under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s directive, Marines in combat arms roles had to hit at least 210 out of 300 points on the Physical Fitness Test using the exact same scoring scale regardless of sex—including a 3-mile run, pull-ups or push-ups, and an abdominal plank.

Now Marine Corps data analyzed by The War Horse shows 91.38% of the 400 female Marines tested in combat specialties passed the new bar, compared to 96.53% of men in those same roles.

Veterans and policy analysts note the sample size is still small and warn that lower raw scores on the male scale could still affect promotions—while supporters say one clear, job-based standard is the fairest way to measure readiness.

Do you think one sex-neutral standard is the right call for all combat roles? Drop your thoughts below. 👇

Cpl. Baughman was deployed with the 187th Infantry Regiment in September 2005 for a year-long deployment to Iraq. On July 17, 2006, Baughman's Humvee was part of a convoy participating in patrol operations in the city of Bayji, Iraq. His Humvee was hit by a RPG, severely injuring him. Later that day, Baughman died from his injuries.

For going beyond the call of duty and for giving his life for his fellow soldiers, on July 19, 2006, Baughman was posthumously awarded the Bronze Star Medal and the Purple Heart.

Small-arms fire rained down on the men of Company F, 2nd Battalion, 23rd Marines. Both Iraqi civilians and Marines were injured. Pinned down, with the injured needing assistance, Sgt. Scott C. Montoya rushed through enemy fire while "repeatedly exposing himself to fire-swept streets," according to his Navy Cross award citation.

Montoya received the U.S. military's second-highest award at Camp Pendleton for heroism stemming from his actions on April 8, 2003, two weeks into Operation Iraqi Freedom.

With his firearm in one hand engaging the enemy and a badly bleeding Marine in the other, he fought their way 500 yards to safety. He returned to the crossfire again and dragged another - who'd been dazed by the concussion of a grenade blast - to a casualty collection point. In all, he rescued four injured Marines and one Iraqi civilian out of harm's way, according to his citation.

Montoya's "extraordinary heroism" arose out of the battle for Baghdad.

Montoya described it this way:

"I saw a hurt Marine, and all my training came into play. It wasn't a cognitive thing; I just saw the situation and cared for my Marines."
Sgt. Jose N. Sanchez, a supply clerk with 2/23, has known Montoya for six years and wasn't surprised when he heard the news.

"The level he went - it's above and beyond the call of anyone, even a Marine," Sanchez said, adding: "What matters to him are his Marines, not the awards or the actions he took."

Montoya received the award in front of family, friends, and the men of his unit. Orange County Sheriff Michael S. Carona was also present.

A deputy sheriff in Orange County, Montoya drew praise from many of his co-workers - including Carona.
"He is a complete warrior," Carona said.

"Whether as a Marine or as a law enforcement figure, he is always putting the community or the country above his own personal safety."

Carona alluded to Montoya's rapid response under fire.

"These things happen in the blink of a second, and an individual has to decide to be a hero or not. He decided to be one."

In the end, Montoya said, “It's just a medal.”

"Service before self is something I teach in the Marine Corps Martial Arts Program," continued Montoya, a MCMAP instructor for his unit. "I feel the award represents the character of the Corps."

Col. Geffery L. Cooper, the battalion's commanding officer during Operation Iraqi Freedom, said Montoya's award was well-deserved.

"It means a great deal to me that the Corps can recognize such Marines of valor in combat,” said Cooper. (Montoya) is a man of integrity and leadership, and his loyalty is unquestionable. He is a great example and advocate for all reservists.”

Excerpts from an article written by Lance Cpl. Daniel J. Redding, The Scout, MCB Camp Pendleton

Hit by enemy fire, he waved the rescue helicopter away.

July 12, 2018. Paktia Province, Afghanistan.

Sgt. 1st Class Christopher A. Celiz was leading a team of Rangers and partnered forces when they came under heavy enemy attack.
A partnered soldier was critically wounded.

Celiz repeatedly exposed himself to intense machine-gun and small-arms fire so the team could move the casualty to the helicopter.
When the aircraft was ready to lift off, he stayed in the open, using his own body as a shield to protect the crew and the wounded man.

Enemy fire finally hit him.
Even then, knowing he was wounded, he waved the helicopter away so it wouldn’t stay under fire trying to load him.

The aircraft escaped.
Celiz did not.

He was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor on December 16, 2021.

A Ranger who put the mission and his teammates above his own survival — right to the end.

Some stories don’t need anything added.

“EVERYTHING YOU SAW ON CNN WITH MY FACE ON IT WAS A LIE. THEY DESTROYED MY LIFE.” — Retired SEAL Team 6 Operator Chris Beck Breaks His Silence on Detransitioning on The Shawn Ryan Show.

Former DEVGRU operator Chris Beck—who was celebrated globally in 2013 as the first openly transgender Navy SEAL—publicly renounced his transition on The Shawn Ryan Show (SRS #050), exposing how media networks and medical systems fast-tracked his transition while ignoring severe combat trauma.

In his own words:

“I had 20 years in the SEAL teams, 13 deployments, a Purple Heart, and a Bronze Star with Valor. When I retired, I was broken physically and mentally, full of severe TBI and trauma.

I walked into the VA, talked to a psychologist for less than an hour, and they handed me hormone pills. No real therapy, no digging into combat trauma—just immediate medical transition.

Within weeks, CNN and every major publication put me on prime-time television. They paraded me around as the face of the movement. I was used. I was naive, in a terribly vulnerable place, and they capitalized on my military credibility to push a political agenda onto American children.

It almost destroyed my life, my health, and my identity.

I am speaking out now to wake people up: I am not a woman. I am a man, a father, and a Navy SEAL. Everything they sold you using my face was propaganda.”

After 20 years in the elite special operations community and 13 combat deployments, Chris Beck is now speaking out to sound the alarm on medical gatekeeping, untreated veteran TBI, and media sensationalism.

What are your thoughts on Chris Beck’s warnings regarding the treatment of combat veterans dealing with severe brain trauma and psychological distress?

MILITARY NEWS — 43 U.S. Army soldiers at Fort Stewart, Georgia reenlisted for two to six more years after their battalion offered a special four-day weekend to play Grand Theft Auto VI on launch day.

Out of 130 eligible troops in the 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion, about one-third took the deal—calling it a "cherry on top" alongside standard retention bonuses that topped $60,000 for at least one soldier.

Would a four-day GTA VI pass convince you to sign another contract? 👇

MIZE, OLA L.

Rank and organization: Master Sergeant (then Sgt.), U.S. Army, Company K, 15th Infantry Regiment, 3d Infantry Division.
Place and date: Near Surang-ni, Korea, 10 to 11 June 1953.
Entered service at: Gadsden, Ala.
G.O. No.: 70, 24 September 1954.

Citation: M/Sgt. Mize, a member of Company K, distinguished himself by conspicuous gallantry and outstanding courage above and beyond the call of duty in action against the enemy. Company K was committed to the defense of "Outpost Harry", a strategically valuable position, when the enemy launched a heavy attack. Learning that a comrade on a friendly listening post had been wounded he moved through the intense barrage, accompanied by a medical aid man, and rescued the wounded soldier. On returning to the main position he established an effective defense system and inflicted heavy casualties against attacks from determined enemy assault forces which had penetrated into trenches within the outpost area. During his fearless actions he was blown down by artillery and grenade blasts 3 times but each time he dauntlessly returned to his position, tenaciously fighting and successfully repelling hostile attacks. When enemy onslaughts ceased, he took his few men and moved from bunker to bunker, firing through apertures and throwing grenades at the foe, neutralizing their positions. When an enemy soldier stepped out behind a comrade, prepared to fire, M/Sgt. Mize killed him, saving the life of his fellow soldier. After rejoining the platoon, moving from man to man, distributing ammunition, and shouting words of encouragement he observed a friendly machine gun position overrun. He immediately fought his way to the position, killing 10 of the enemy and dispersing the remainder. Fighting back to the command post, and finding several friendly wounded there, he took a position to protect them. Later, securing a radio, he directed friendly artillery fire upon the attacking enemy's routes of approach. At dawn he helped regroup for a counterattack which successfully drove the enemy from the outpost. M/Sgt. Mize's valorous conduct and unflinching courage reflect lasting glory upon himself and uphold the noble traditions of the military service.

Matthew Gene "Axe" Axelson (June 25, 1976 – June 28, 2005) was a United States Navy SEAL who was killed in the War in Afghanistan. He was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross for his actions and valor during Operation Red Wings, in which he was killed. He served in that operation along with Michael Murphy, Daniel Dietz, and Marcus Luttrell. Dietz and Luttrell were also awarded the Navy Cross, the Purple Heart, and the Navy good conduct medals, where Murphy received the Medal of Honor.

Citation: For extraordinary heroism in actions against the enemy while serving in a four-man Special Reconnaissance element with SEAL Delivery Vehicle Team ONE, Naval Special Warfare Task unit, Afghanistan from 27 to 28 June 2005. Petty Officer Axelson demonstrated extraordinary heroism in the face of grave danger in the vicinity of Asadabad, Konar Province, Afghanistan. Operating in the middle of an enemy-controlled area, in extremely rugged terrain, his Special Reconnaissance element was tasked with locating a high-level Anti-Coalition Militia leader, in support of a follow-on direct action mission to disrupt enemy activity. On 28 June 2005, the element was spotted by Anti-Coalition Militia sympathizers, who immediately revealed their position to the militia fighters. As a result, the element directly encountered the enemy. Demonstrating exceptional resolve and fully understanding the gravity of the situation, Petty Officer Axelson's element bravely engaged the militia, who held both a numerical and positional advantage. The ensuing firefight resulted in numerous enemy personnel killed, with several of the Navy members suffering casualties. Ignoring his injuries and demonstrating exceptional composure, Petty Officer Axelson advised the teammate closest to him to escape while he provided cover fire. With total disregard for his own life and thinking only of his teammate's survival, he continued to attack the enemy, eliminating additional militia fighters, until he was mortally wounded by enemy fire. A champion of freedom, Petty Officer Axelson will be remembered for his self-sacrificing actions in the continuing Global War on Terrorism. By his undaunted courage, fortitude under fire, and unwavering dedication to duty, Petty Officer Axelson reflected great credit upon himself and upheld the highest traditions of the United States Naval Service. He gallantly gave his life for the cause of freedom.

"For 150 years, horse-drawn carriages have been a fixture of Central Park. Today, we are bringing that chapter to a close," Mamdani said at Thursday's signing.

The U.S. just test-fired an ICBM… one day before major nuclear talks. 

Late on November 17, an unarmed Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missile launched from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.

The missile has been in service for 56 years.
This was a routine operational test, the Air Force says — scheduled years in advance and not tied to any current events.

Still, the timing is hard to ignore.
The launch came just as high-level nuclear and diplomatic talks were about to begin.

Officials insist it’s pure coincidence.
Critics and observers are asking the obvious question:
Coincidence… or message?

These tests happen regularly to verify the reliability of the aging Minuteman III force.
But when they land this close to sensitive negotiations, people notice.

What do you think — scheduled routine, or deliberate signal?

The National Security Agency is reportedly experiencing a third consecutive day of internal communications outages, according to Fox News.

While sources say the agency can still communicate internally, the ongoing disruption is being described as "highly unusual." Earlier this week, an NSA spokesperson pointed to "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance" and stressed that mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational.

With recent disruptions also hitting the FAA, Microsoft, major U.S. banks, and the IRS, officials say rapid patching and system upgrades—not a cyberattack—are to blame. Do you buy the routine maintenance explanation?

#NSA #NationalSecurity #CyberSecurity

Before Hollywood knew him from Star Wars or Marriage Story, Adam Driver was an 81mm mortarman in the U.S. Marine Corps.

Motivated by the 9/11 attacks, he enlisted and served for two years and eight months with 1st Battalion, 1st Marines at Camp Pendleton—training to deploy to Iraq until a fractured sternum from a mountain biking accident led to a medical discharge in 2004 at the rank of Lance Corporal.

He later co-founded Arts in the Armed Forces to bring free live theater to service members around the world. Did you know Driver served in the Marines?

#AdamDriver #USMarines #USMC

Russia just flew nuclear-capable bombers past Japan… and landed them in Vietnam. 

On November 17, Japan reported that two suspected Russian aircraft briefly entered its airspace.
Fighters were scrambled.

Those aircraft turned out to be Tu-95 bombers — the same long-range, nuclear-capable platforms Russia has used for decades to probe defenses and send signals.

The bombers continued south and later landed in Da Nang, Vietnam.
A rare deployment that far from home.

Moscow is showing it can still project strategic aviation power deep into the Indo-Pacific, even while fighting a major war in Europe.
Japan sees it as a provocation.
Vietnam is hosting the aircraft without public comment so far.

For the United States, the question is straightforward:
Is this just routine muscle-flexing… or another reminder that Russia is actively working the Pacific theater while everyone’s attention is split?

Should America worry?

The remarks come as Trump, Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping held a landmark trilateral meeting in Shenzhen—while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy voiced concern about any potential deal being discussed without Kyiv at the table.

Can diplomacy end the war in Ukraine, or are the sides still too far apart? Share your take below.

Kenneth Braun served as a Navy Corpsman alongside the Maines of India 3/9. At the Battle of Getlin’s Corner, the 19 year old Doc saved the lives of at least 35 Marines. He received the Navy Cross for his actions in 2005, 38 years after the battle.
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
The unit came under heavy attack on the night of March 30, 1967. Marines fell everywhere as mortars, grenades, and machine gun fire rained down on their exposed position on the side of a hill. An NVA force more than five times the size of India Company moved into the attack. They shot Marine wounded in the head as they passed them. Ignoring painful shrapnel wounds, Doc Braun sprinted forward to every call of, “Corpsman up!”
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
The company moved up the hill away from the NVA. Braun ignored orders to keep himself concealed in the elephant grass, and rushed back down over and over. He treated Marine after Marine and dragged them to safety. On multiple occasions, he encountered NVA in the grass, but managed to kill them first.
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
Doc Braun located Lt John Bobo (Medal of Honor winner) as he single-handedly fought off the NVA in his area. Bobo’s leg was blown off below the knee. Braun cinched a web belt around the leg as a tourniquet and dragged Bobo up the hill. After 15 yards, they stopped to return fire. Braun stuffed the stump of Bobo’s leg into the ground to stunt the bleeding. An NVA soldier crept behind the Marines and let loose with his machine gun. Bobo was killed instantly. Doc Braun was hit three times in his back, exposing his spine. He managed to crawl up the hill to the Marines’ consolidated position. He coached his squad leader through patching up the holes in his back, and gave himself a shot of morphine. The squad leader later described Braun as “Superman,” having wounds that should have killed any man, and taking them without a single moan or sound of pain.
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
While they waited for the next attack, a Huey gunship arrived and wreaked havoc on the NVA. Braun was evacuated to a hospital ship, and eventually medically retired due to his wounds. The Navy Cross he received in 2005 added to his Bronze Star with “V” and two Purple Hearts.

Sgt. Philip A. McCulloch, Jr.
3rd Battalion, 5th Marines
Sangin, Afghanistan, Jan. 2011
Award: Silver Star

During a six-hour engagement with insurgent forces in the Sangin District, Sgt. McCulloch led his squad of Marines in a determined pursuit of a numerically superior enemy force. After being attacked by enemy fighters, he personally led his squad's counter attack by assuming point and closing on the enemy, pausing just long enough to destroy an enemy fighting positions with an AT-4. Once he regained the initiative, he pursued the enemy into a nearby row of compounds and forced them into fixed positions where many of them were destroyed by close air support and indirect fires, combined with maneuver ... Throughout the engagement, he aggressively drove his Marines to remain focused, exposing himself to enemy fire to identify enemy positions and coordinate fires in support of maneuver. Even after beginning to return to base, as the enemy again engaged the Marines, he controlled another section of helicopters with devastating effects, allowing his squad to return to friendly lines." (U.S. Marine Corps photo by Lance Cpl. Eric Quintanilla)

He was the voice of Bambi.
Then he became a Marine… and never told his troops. 

As a little boy, Donnie Dunagan was the voice of young Bambi in the classic Disney film.
That soft, innocent voice millions of kids grew up hearing.

Years later he joined the Marine Corps.
He served three tours in Vietnam.
He earned a Bronze Star and three Purple Hearts.

And almost no one in his units knew about the Disney connection.
He kept it quiet.
No stories about the movie set. No “hey, I was Bambi.”
Just a Marine doing the job.

Maj. Donnie Dunagan passed away on November 4 at the age of 92.

From the voice of a cartoon deer to a combat Marine who earned three Purple Hearts…
and chose not to trade on the fame.

Some people live two completely different lives and somehow make both of them count.

Rest easy, Major.

Jennifer M. Moreno. Moreno was assigned to a U.S. Army Ranger unit in Afghanistan. On Oct. 5, 2013, she was killed in action during a patrol that would take the lives of two Army Rangers.

During a Special Operations raid in Zhari District (Afghanistan), when a suicide bomber initiated an ambush in the compound the army team was entering. During the twelve additional blasts that injured 30 Rangers and killed three, Moreno chose to not follow stand-by procedure in order to give essential medical assistance to a fellow soldier trapped nearby, which resulted in the triggering of another IED that led to her death at the age of 25. She was posthumously promoted to captain and awarded the Purple Heart, Combat Action Badge and Bronze Star.

Is Everyone Overreacting to the 2026 Midterms?You’ve probably seen the posts calling this election a historic disaster for Republicans.
But take a look at the actual House numbers:Bill Clinton lost 54 seats in 1994  
Barack Obama lost 63 seats in 2010  
Donald Trump just lost 41 seats in 2026

Forty-one is a clear loss. No question.
But it’s not the biggest midterm seat drop in recent decades. Presidents almost always lose seats in the House during midterms. That’s been the pattern for a long time.So when people treat 41 seats like the end of the world, it feels a bit overblown if you’re only looking at the House.That said, the full picture is more complicated.
Democrats also flipped the Senate and won some surprising races in traditionally red states. Those results matter and give the other side real momentum.Still, the pure House seat count that everyone’s screaming about isn’t as unprecedented as the reactions suggest.

The 52-year-old former Green Beret shared the tribute during his visit to Lebanon, honoring the 241 Americans killed in the Oct. 23, 1983 Beirut barracks bombing.

Matthew Gene "Axe" Axelson (June 25, 1976 – June 28, 2005) was a United States Navy SEAL who was killed in the War in Afghanistan. He was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross for his actions and valor during Operation Red Wings, in which he was killed. He served in that operation along with Michael Murphy, Daniel Dietz, and Marcus Luttrell. Dietz and Luttrell were also awarded the Navy Cross, the Purple Heart, and the Navy good conduct medals, where Murphy received the Medal of Honor.

Citation: For extraordinary heroism in actions against the enemy while serving in a four-man Special Reconnaissance element with SEAL Delivery Vehicle Team ONE, Naval Special Warfare Task unit, Afghanistan from 27 to 28 June 2005. Petty Officer Axelson demonstrated extraordinary heroism in the face of grave danger in the vicinity of Asadabad, Konar Province, Afghanistan. Operating in the middle of an enemy-controlled area, in extremely rugged terrain, his Special Reconnaissance element was tasked with locating a high-level Anti-Coalition Militia leader, in support of a follow-on direct action mission to disrupt enemy activity. On 28 June 2005, the element was spotted by Anti-Coalition Militia sympathizers, who immediately revealed their position to the militia fighters. As a result, the element directly encountered the enemy. Demonstrating exceptional resolve and fully understanding the gravity of the situation, Petty Officer Axelson's element bravely engaged the militia, who held both a numerical and positional advantage. The ensuing firefight resulted in numerous enemy personnel killed, with several of the Navy members suffering casualties. Ignoring his injuries and demonstrating exceptional composure, Petty Officer Axelson advised the teammate closest to him to escape while he provided cover fire. With total disregard for his own life and thinking only of his teammate's survival, he continued to attack the enemy, eliminating additional militia fighters, until he was mortally wounded by enemy fire. A champion of freedom, Petty Officer Axelson will be remembered for his self-sacrificing actions in the continuing Global War on Terrorism. By his undaunted courage, fortitude under fire, and unwavering dedication to duty, Petty Officer Axelson reflected great credit upon himself and upheld the highest traditions of the United States Naval Service. He gallantly gave his life for the cause of freedom.

“VIOLENT STORM OVERWHELMED VESSEL: AIR FORCE EOD JUMPMASTER SAVES DROWNING SURVIVORS AT SEA.”

When a violent ocean storm hit with mountainous swells, freezing temperatures, and treacherous rip currents, people were thrown into the open sea and within minutes of drowning. Senior Master Sergeant Joseph Riemer dove straight in.

An elite Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) flight leader and the first EOD technician in U.S. Air Force history to earn the Military Freefall Jumpmaster Badge, Riemer was at sea when disaster struck:

Hearing desperate cries for help, Riemer immediately plunged into the freezing, turbulent ocean, battling massive swells and rip currents to reach the scattered victims.

Reaching the survivors, Riemer used water survival techniques to keep them afloat, quickly assessing that two airmen had exhausted their strength and were moments away from slipping beneath the surface.

Fighting Back with Flotation Gear: Riemer fought his way back through the punishing waves to the boat, retrieved emergency life preservers, swam back into the violent sea, and secured the drowning victims in flotation vests.

 Swimming against powerful currents, he towed the victims through the swells to within 25 meters of the vessel, secured a heavy safety line, and hauled them safely aboard before ensuring everyone was accounted for on the return to port.

In March 2025, Brigadier General Brian Hartless presented Senior Master Sergeant Joseph Riemer with the Airman’s Medal—the Department of the Air Force's highest decoration for heroism outside of combat.

A combat veteran of Operations Enduring Freedom, Inherent Resolve, and Freedom's Sentinel, Riemer currently serves as the Senior Enlisted Leader for the Air Force Civil Engineer Center EOD Division at Tyndall Air Force Base, where he was also named the 2024 AFMC Outstanding EOD Master Blaster of the Year.

The Navy is discontinuing the peacoat after more than a century. 

That heavy, double-breasted wool coat has been part of the Navy’s look for generations.
Starting October 1, 2027, it will no longer be authorized.

For a lot of people who served, the peacoat wasn’t just a coat.
It was the thing you put on when the weather got nasty, the one that showed up in photos, the one that felt like the Navy.

Now it’s being phased out for something lighter, more practical, and easier to maintain.

Tradition versus efficiency.
Another small piece of the old Navy is moving into history.

Sfc. Hester is one of the few women to be awarded for valor in close-quarters combat.

Leigh Ann Hester was a sergeant with the National Guard’s Kentucky-based 617th Military Police Company when she was deployed to Iraq, and in 2005, she was scanning and clearing a route for a supply convoy near Baghdad when her squad was ambushed by enemy fire.

She was trained for this, as it was a risk that came with her daily job in Iraq. Thus, when they became under attack, she knew exactly what to do. She directed her team away from the enemy’s intense fire and into a flanking position that exposed multiple irrigation ditches and an orchard that the enemies were using to stage the attack.

She was initially directing fire, then began fighting on foot. Sgt. Hester displayed incredible bravery as she had walked directly into the line of fire to kill at least three enemy combatants at close range, resulting in numerous convoy members lives saved. With thirty-three insurgents killed or wounded and one captured, every member of her unit survived.

Her heroic actions led her to become the first woman since World War II to earn the Silver Star Medal and the very first to ever earn it for combat valor.
Sgt. Hester separated from the National Guard and became a police officer after she returned to the United States; a job she had wanted since childhood. But she enjoyed being a soldier so much so, that she rejoined the National Guard shortly after.

In 2014, she spent 18 months in Afghanistan, where she was promoted to sergeant first class. And in 2017, she was sent to the Virgin Islands as part of the international humanitarian effort in the wake of Hurricane Maria.

Captain Kent Solheim, United States Army, was awarded the Silver Star for actions during a raid in Karbala, Iraq where he courageously saved multiple American lives by disregarding his personal safety.

On July 27, 2007, Captain Kent Solheim, United States Army, participated in Operation VOLCANO II, an operation designed to capture a senior leader of the infamous Shiite militia, the Mahdi Army in the city of Karbala, Iraq. Solheim's team "fast roped" from helicopters into the area, and set up their position near the target building. Insurgents viciously attacked the American forces from three sides with rocketpropelled grenades (RPGs) and AK-47s. As the enemy fire got heavier, combat air support was called in to eliminate some of the aggressors, but a significant number of attackers remained to the north of Solheim and his unit. These insurgents used the dust that the assault force's helicopters had kicked up to conceal their movements.
With the insurgents targeting one of the American positions, Solheim aggressively maneuvered his men to reinforce the beleaguered soldiers. It was then that he noticed an insurgent armed with an RPG, less than ten meters away from his position. Disregarding any concern for himself, he bravely charged forward, shot and killed the insurgent, saving the Americans in the nick of time. Realizing that the US forces in the building were in grave danger, Solheim exposed himself to enemy fire in order to gain a better position to cover the other soldiers in his unit. From this location, he managed to limit the insurgent fire on his team. In the final moments of the engagement he rounded a corner and he found himself face to face with an AK-47-wielding Mahdi fighter. Solheim made a split second decision, firing at and killing the insurgent. However, as the terrorist fell to the ground fatally wounded, he let loose one last burst from his AK-47, which wounded Solheim in the legs and back

On 8 June 2004 then First Lieutenant Christopher Niedziocha's convoy came under heavy rocket and small arms fire in an enemy ambush near the village of Sandabuz, Afghanistan. Niedziocha pushed his vehicles through the kill zone as far forward as possible to confront the enemy's main ambush site. With his vehicles caught in a crossfire, he led his Marines from the front by engaging enemy positions with devastating heavy machine gun and small arms fire.

Niedziocha aggressively engaged the enemy at a distance of less than 100 meters and negated the enemy's advantage of standoff and surprise. Seeking to regain the initiative, he led his Marines in a bold flanking maneuver, trapping some enemy forces who were later found and eliminated, causing others to break contact. He then led his Marines in pursuit of the fleeing enemy, neutralizing the remaining enemy forces with direct fire and close air support."

For his bold initiative and decisive action, Niedziocha was awarded the Silver Star.

The Air Force just trained 1,518 new pilots in one year — the most since 1991.

More capacity. Faster pipeline. Same standards.

“United States Marine Corps Corporal Ryan L. Ice was young, active, and full of life—having served faithfully in Okinawa, Japan, and here in Florida—before stage 4 colon cancer stole everything from him. Above everything else, Ryan was fiercely loyal as a friend, a son, and a brother, and even more so as a husband. We shared a once-in-a-lifetime type of love. 

We had only been married for 10 days when our entire world collapsed. Ryan was diagnosed with stage 4 colon adenocarcinoma that had aggressively spread to his liver, lungs, and stomach lining, complicated by painful ascites and recurring pleural effusions. Overnight, our newlywed life became hospital rooms, chemo chairs, and endless IV poles. 

People often look at cancer through a sanitized lens, so I want to be honest about what he endured: chemo isn't inspiring or pretty. It is literal poison, total exhaustion, and a suffocating anxiety underneath every single moment. Yet even on our darkest, hardest days, Ryan and I strived to maintain a positive attitude—not because we weren't terrified, but because we refused to let the disease take away our love or our spirit. 

Ryan passed away on November 3, 2026. Before he left us, it was deeply important to him that we use his voice to advocate for early colon cancer screenings. He didn't want other young, healthy service members or civilians to assume they are invincible or wait until it is too late. 

Please don't ignore your body, push for the tests, and get screened early. In honor of Cpl. Ryan L. Ice—my best friend, my husband, and my hero. Semper Fi.💔” -G. O’Toole

74 years ago today, one American pilot took on seven Soviet MiGs… alone. 

November 18, 1952.
Navy Lieutenant Royce Williams was flying an F9F Panther off the coast of Korea when he suddenly found himself facing seven Soviet MiG-15s.

Outnumbered.
Outmatched in speed and climb.
And completely alone.

For 35 minutes — the longest dogfight in U.S. Navy history — Williams fought them.
He shot down four of the Soviet jets.
His plane was hit by a 37mm cannon shell, hydraulics failing, yet he still made it back to the carrier and landed.

Because the enemy pilots were Soviet (not North Korean or Chinese), the entire engagement was classified.
Williams was ordered to keep quiet.
He did — for more than 50 years.

Only after the Cold War ended did the full story come out.
In February of this year, at age 100, he finally received the Medal of Honor.
He is now 101.

One man.
Seven enemy jets.
Four confirmed kills.
And a secret kept for half a century.

Some stories still stop you cold.

“144 VESSELS REDIRECTED.” — U.S. Central Command Tightens Grip on the Strait of Hormuz Amid High-Stakes Iran Talks.

Amid ongoing diplomatic negotiations between the United States and Iran regarding security and administration across the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed that coalition and U.S. naval forces have now intercepted and redirected 144 commercial vessels under the renewed maritime blockade of traffic to and from Iranian ports.

The maritime enforcement surge comes at a pivotal diplomatic juncture:

• The Chokepoint at Stake: The Strait of Hormuz remains the world's most critical maritime energy corridor, handling roughly 20% of global petroleum transit. Control and administration of these shipping lanes remain the central sticking point in ongoing U.S.-Iran discussions.

• Enforcing the Blockade: U.S. Navy carrier strike groups, guided-missile destroyers, and maritime patrol aircraft have maintained continuous overwatch, conducting visit-board-search-and-seizure (VBSS) operations and turning back non-compliant vessels and illicit "shadow fleet" tankers attempting to evade sanctions.

• Diplomatic Leverage: By cutting off commercial cargo and petroleum shipping routes to Iranian ports, Washington is applying maximum operational pressure on Tehran while negotiating maritime protocols and regional de-escalation terms.

“12,000 FEET UP A FROZEN MOUNTAIN: HE CARRIED HIS PARALYZED TEAMMATE DOWN TO AN IMPROVISED LZ.”

High-altitude mountain rescue leaves zero room for error. When a catastrophic fall in the Colorado backcountry left a Green Beret paralyzed and freezing, Sergeant First Class Bobby Haran stabilized the traumatic injuries, rigged a descent system, and hauled his teammate down a sheer rock face to an area where a rescue chopper could touch its skids.

At the summit of the 14,023-foot Wilson Peak near Telluride, Colorado, SFC Robert "Bobby" Haran an elite mountain instructor with the Special Operations Mountain Warfare Training Center (10th Special Forces Group) watched his teammate’s lead ski strike a submerged rock, releasing the binding and triggering an uncontrolled, 2,000-foot plunge down an icy couloir.

What followed was one of the most remarkable acts of alpine mountaineering and survival in Special Operations history:

Knowing that skiing the steep route solo risked triggering massive avalanches onto his injured partner, Haran descended 2,200 vertical feet on foot across near-vertical ice using only crampons and an ice axe, hauling his teammate's recovered skis to use as an emergency litter.

Reaching his teammate, Haran found him suffering from a fractured sternum, broken hip, shattered shoulder, compound leg fractures, internal bleeding, a torn aorta, and severe hypothermia. Haran stabilized his breathing and wounds in sub-zero winds.

Communicating via emergency satellite with San Miguel County Search and Rescue, Haran rigged a lowering system and moved his paralyzed teammate hundreds of feet further down sheer rock to an improvised alpine landing zone.

After a rescue helicopter hoisted the casualty to St. Mary's Hospital in Grand Junction, Haran skied the remaining backcountry miles solo back to the trailhead.

During a formal ceremony at Fort Carson, Major General Lawrence G. Ferguson presented the Soldier's Medal—the Army's highest peacetime decoration for heroism—to honor Haran's extraordinary valor and skill.

“Bobby, without a doubt, is the only individual that comes to mind that could have performed the way he did that day,” Haran’s NCOIC concluded. “Because of all his training, perseverance, and wherewithal, it resulted in him saving his teammate's life.”

“ONE ROUND. 70 FEET IN THE PITCH DARK. UNDER HEAVY RIFLE FIRE.” — Engaging an active long rifle from behind cover across 23 yards in total darkness using only a standard duty handgun is nearly impossible under live-fire stress. Wounded in the leg by an AR-15 ambush that took the lives of his two partners, Officer Alec Iurato stabilized his breathing, used a patrol cruiser as a shooting platform, and fired the single 9mm shot that ended the gunfight.

“Officer Iurato was confronted with an active, heavily armed shooter who had already killed two police officers and fired more than 80 rounds from an assault rifle. Despite suffering a severe gunshot wound to his leg, Officer Iurato took cover, evaluated the threat, and fired a single precision shot from approximately 70 feet away that neutralized the gunman. His actions were justified, heroic, and saved countless lives.”

 The 70-Foot Shot
The Coordinated Ambush: On October 12, 2022, three officers from the Bristol Police Department responded to a staged 911 call on Redstone Hill Road. As they approached, a gunman concealed in the darkness ambushed them with a semi-automatic AR-15 rifle, firing over 80 rounds of high-velocity ammunition in seconds.

Sergeant Dustin DeMonte and Officer Alex Hamzy were mortally wounded in the initial volley. Both heroes were posthumously promoted to Lieutenant and Sergeant for their ultimate sacrifice protecting the Bristol community.

Officer Iurato sustained a devastating gunshot wound when a rifle round struck his lower leg. Refusing to freeze in the kill zone, he crawled through the dark toward a parked cruiser, placing an engine block and tire between himself and the incoming rounds.

 Body-worn camera audio captures Iurato methodically regulating his respirations while rifle rounds ricocheted off the street. Staging his handgun over the cruiser’s rear quarter panel, he acquired his sights in the darkness, tracked the gunman at roughly 70 feet (23 yards), and broke a single 9mm trigger press directly into the shooter’s head, ending the ambush instantly.

The Fallacy of Handgun Limitations: Standard tactical doctrine often considers handguns effective only within 7 to 15 yards under combat stress. Iurato proved that solid fundamentals—grip, sight picture, and trigger discipline can make a standard service pistol lethal at extended rifle ranges.

Controlling the Stress Inoculation Curve: High-stress gunfights induce intense adrenaline dumps, tunnel vision, and auditory exclusion. Controlling breath tempo under cover resets heart rate just enough to execute precision motor skills.

Exploiting Improvised Hard Cover: Vehicles offer limited ballistic protection from high-velocity rifle fire, but the wheels, axles, and engine block provide substantial cover and a rigid shooting rest for stabilizing long-range pistol fire.

April 24, 2012 Dallas, TX, Army Spc. Philip C.S. Schiller, was laid to rest with full Military Honors at the DFW National Cemetery.

He was a 2010 graduate of The Colony High School — died April 11, 2012 in Kandahar province, Afghanistan, while defending his unit despite his own mortal chest wound.

Bronze Star Medal Relatives of troop members who were in the battle told his family that Spc. Schiller continued to provide machine gun cover for his unit during an enemy attack. He received the Bronze Star and the Purple Heart for his actions.

Spc. Schiller was born in Hartford, Conn., and grew up in nearby Barkhamsted. In 2009 he moved to The Colony to live with his sister, Courtney Schiller. "My brother was a fun-loving person and wanted to always help everyone in every way he could," his sister was quoted in a local paper, and said. "He was my best friend."

She talked to her brother by telephone six days before he was killed.

He had visited North Texas last month, before his deployment.

During his senior year at The Colony High School, Spc. Schiller participated in JROTC. Spc. Schiller enlisted a few weeks after he graduated from high school and completed basic training at Fort Benning, Ga., in August 2010. He was assigned to the Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Wash., that fall and was deployed to Afghanistan in March 2012.

He joined the Army ... because he wanted to be a police officer when he got out. That was his dream," his sister said.

In addition to his sister, Spc. Schiller is survived by his mother, Robin Larsen of Dallas; his father, Erik Schiller of Winsted, Conn.; and three grandparents.
